name: Salas

new_statements.quote: Betonung. Die Worte werden stets auf der vorletzten Silbe betont. Steht ein Diphthong an letzter Stelle, so erhält er den Ton, da er als zweisilbig empfunden wird. Steht er an vorletzter Stelle, so liegt der Ton doch auf dem ersten Vokal des Diphthongen, da darin gerade die Eigentümlichkeit der Diphthonge liegt. Ausnahmen: lósina Mörser, lúmaa Pfeil, kwália Kessel, mítawa groß, bebéila Blitz, úfeia (neben ufa) Haus, kanamúmala Sagorührer, mul-mátana Feuerplatz, néila männlich, ínana weiblich, maléena Himmel, [...] ibané wo?, keintér zerbrechen, ubós küssen, mumatá unreif sein, masanán abends, kisé selbst
new_statements.translation: Stress. Words are always stressed on the penultimate syllable. If a diphthong stands in final position it receives the stress, since it is felt to be disyllabic. If it stands in penultimate position, the stress nevertheless lies on the first vowel of the diphthong, since precisely therein lies the peculiarity of the diphthongs. Exceptions: lósina 'mortar', lúmaa 'arrow', kwália 'kettle', mítawa 'big', bebéila 'lightning', úfeia (beside ufa) 'house', kanamúmala 'sago stirrer', mul-mátana 'fireplace', néila 'male', ínana 'female', maléena 'sky', [...] ibané 'where?', keintér 'break', ubós 'kiss', mumatá 'be unripe', masanán 'in the evening', kisé 'self'.
new_statements.citation: Tauern, Odo D. 1931. Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Sprachen und Dialekte von Seran (Schluss). Anthropos 26(1/2): 109-139; section 'Liambata-Dialekt der Alfuren von Ostseran. Bonfia-Sprache.', Lautlehre.
new_statements.locator: p.130, 'Lautlehre', paragraph 'Betonung' (p.146 of the archive.org issue scan); cf. p.129 on vowel length and diphthong accent
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ) at p.146 = printed p.130 and the 200-dpi render. Steht ein Diphthong an letzter Stelle, so erhaelt er den Ton, da er als zweisilbig empfunden wird. Steht er an vorletzter Stelle, so liegt der Ton doch auf dem ersten Vokal des Diphthongen..' followed by 'Ausnahmen:' losina, lumaa, kwalia, mitawa, bebeila, ufeia, kanamumala, mul-matana, neila, inana, maleena, selefa, larana, salaana, baria, fotaa, simais, raus, ibane, keinter, ubos, mumata, masanan, kise, all accent-marked); the compiler [..] elides only the middle of the exception list. p.145 = printed p.129 also carries '…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable. A word-final diphthong (ai ei oi au ou) counts as two syllables, so stress lands on its first vowel (surface-final); a penultimate diphthong is stressed on its first element. Stress does not condition vowel length (p.129). A closed list of about 28 words is lexically marked as exceptional, mostly antepenultimate on vowel-final trisyllables (lósina, mítawa, sélefa..) and final on a few consonant- or e-final words (keintér, ubós, masanán, ibané, kisé).
new_statements.exceptions: Explicit 'Ausnahmen' list p.130 (accent-marked): lósina, lúmaa, kwália, mítawa, bebéila, úfeia, kanamúmala, mul-mátana, néila, ínana, maléena, sélefa, lárana, saláana, bária, fótaa, simaís, raús, ibané, keintér, ubós, mumatá, masanán, kisé; diphthong-final words take final stress by rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation forms in a short field grammar (Tauern's own fieldwork on Seram, 1910s; author notes the material is incomplete, p.128-129). On the identity of the variety: the variety is Tauern's 'Liambata/Bonfia' of East Seram, only tentatively equated with Salas [sgu] (see the note on which variety); Grimes & Edwards 2026 explicitly decline to identify any extant data as Salas.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Tauern 1931: 128-139) describes the 'Liambata-Dialekt der Alfuren von Ostseran / Bonfia-Sprache', located by Tauern 'oestlich des Aketernate-Flusses.. im ganzen Ostseran'. Its identity with sala1269 is only tentative: Loski & Loski 1989: 121 'Tauern (1931) presents a short grammar of Liambata, possibly a dialect of Salas Gunung'; Ethnologue/OLAC list 'Liambata' and 'Lenkaitahe' as alternate names of Salas [sgu]; but Grimes & Edwards 2026: 342 judge Tauern's Liambata 'related to but different from Seti.. we cannot confidently identify any Salas data', p.419 'may represent Salas [sgu] or a variety of Benggoi [bgy]' (beng1287), and their gazetteer files 'Liambata' under Liana-Seti [ste] (lian1255). Stresemann's 1927 'Liambata' is a different dataset (= Wallace 1869 'Ahtiago', a Seti variety). Any catalog entry for sala1269 built on this quote must carry an identity-uncertain flag (Salas ?= Tauern's Liambata; alternatives beng1287 / lian1255). Note that Tauern's other East Seram sketch in the same article (Uhei-Kahlakim = Seti/Benggoi, p.123) states the same penultimate rule, so the stress value is areally consistent whichever identification holds.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress: every Seram variety Tauern describes (Wemale 1928:1003, Makabala 1929:953, Lissabata 1929:963, Uhei-Kahlakim 1931:123, Liambata/Bonfia 1931:130) is penultimate with accent-marked lexical exceptions, and no other source held by the project (Loski & Loski 1989, Collins 1986, Grimes & Edwards 2026, Badan Bahasa Peta Bahasa) says anything about Salas stress. The disagreement is about identity, not placement: Loski & Loski 1989:121 call Tauern's Liambata 'possibly a dialect of Salas Gunung' and Ethnologue/OLAC list Liambata as an alternate name of Salas [sgu], whereas Grimes & Edwards 2026:342, 419 say Tauern's Liambata may be a Seti variety or Benggoi [bgy] and that no Salas data can be confidently identified.

sources.note: Liambata/Bonfia Lautlehre p.130: words always stressed on the penultimate syllable; a word-final diphthong takes the stress (felt as disyllabic); a penultimate diphthong is stressed on its first vowel; p.129 stress does not affect vowel length; closed list of ~28 accent-marked lexical exceptions (lósina, lúmaa, mítawa, úfeia.. ibané, keintér, ubós, mumatá, masanán, kisé). Uhei-Kahlakim (Seti/Benggoi) p.123: penultimate with few marked exceptions, except when the final syllable is a diphthong.

sources.note: Editor's English rendering of Le Cocq d'Armandville's notes: words of more than two syllables are usually stressed on the penult; in disyllables stress is 'sometimes' final even after a long penult (serga, Laura > Laurá-type examples, mister pronounced like French mystere), while disyllables whose first syllable has i, o or oe are said always to stress that (penultimate) syllable, pronounced long; the list marks stress with accents (editorial note on stress marking follows).
